doc.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Four years with Sammy Davis and Louie Bellson
summary: Working for Sammy Davis Jr. from 1972 to 1976 was the most fun job; he got in via Berlin and Paris concerts and recalls Louie Bellson from the Dorsey band.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: Yeah. I mean I went out for four years, 1972 to ’76 with Sammy, mainly because it was so much fun. It was probably the most fun job I’ve ever had in my life.

Yeah. I mean he and I had a thing going there that was just — I couldn’t wait to get on the stand at night. Because it kept growing. It started off and the guitar had a lot of things with him when I first joined the thing, and then gradually the guitar was put aside and the piano came in and then pretty soon about half of the show was just him and piano. And it was a challenge all the time. The people would shout a request to him, a tune he didn’t know and I didn’t know, and we’d try to do it. And it was so much fun. He had a great statement which could apply to jazz or anything else when he said, “we ain’t doing Hamlet up here, have fun.” And there was never a night that we didn’t have fun. I mean originally I went with him just for a couple of concerts. His conductor called me and this was 1972 right after I decided I was going to bounce the studios and just play piano when and where I liked, and then I get this call. He said, “we’ve got a couple of concerts next week, would you like to do them?” I didn’t even ask about money or anything else. I said, “fine.” He said, “well the first one’s in Berlin, the other one is in Paris.” I said, “fine, send me a ticket.” And the plane was like twelve hours late so I got there about maybe an hour and a half ahead of the concert, went in and read his whole book that night. But at

that time my reading was good so it was no problem. And then when I came back after the two concerts I thought well that’s it. Then I got a call from him and Louie Bellson was playing drums on both the concerts there, and Louie’s an old friend because he was with the Dorsey band when I was there, and we traveled together. I bought a convertible and he and I would travel away from the band, because he’s a non-smoker, non-drinker also, and we couldn’t stand it. I went on the bus once, that was it, with the booze and the smoke, I said I can’t make this, I’ve got to be out in the open. So I said, “Lou, you want to drive?” He said, “yeah.” He would sit in the back seat of the convertible with a drum pad and practice while I’m driving you know. That’s why he’s as good as he is. He really took some time. He had that drum pad with him all the time. And as good as he played then, he was still practicing all the time.
